title: Phase-DGS: Phase-Guided Dynamic Gaussian Splatting from Unsynchronized Multi-view Video
claim: Replacing timestamps with a learned semantic phase aligns unsynchronized streams, so frames in the same motion state correspond across sources.
layout: 2 panels: top-left timeline and pipeline flowing downward then right, top-right phase plot
description: Panel (a) opens with three color-coded timeline bars for Cam01 to Cam03. Each bar is split into motion segments such as Run, Jumping, Landing, Off, Freeze and Drop. The bars are misaligned in time, and a vertical dotted line marks the same frame index f_th. Arrows drop from that line to three photos of two people, one per camera, with Cam03 outlined in red. The photos feed a yellow 'Phase extraction module', which outputs phases p1, p2 and p3. Those phases go into a '4DGS Trainer' box that shows colored Gaussian ellipses with motion arrows. The trainer outputs a rendered image. Panel (b) is a dashed box with a phase-versus-frame plot. It has red, blue and green lines for the three cameras, showing offset, freeze (flat) and drop (jump). Points p1 = p3 and p2 are marked at f_th.
caption: Conceptual diagram of Phase-DGS. (a) In an unsynchronized multi-view dataset, images sharing the frame index are actually captured at different time instants. The proposed phase extraction module estimates an inherent semantic phase from each input image, which is then used to train 4DGS. (b) The graph shows the estimated phases across cameras. When a sequence is offset, the phase shifts along the x-axis direction; when frozen, the phase is predicted parallel to the x-axis; and when dropped, the phase is predicted parallel to the y-axis.
abstract: Spatiotemporal scene reconstruction with Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (DGS) fundamentally depends on perfect temporal synchronization across all cameras, an assumption rarely achievable in practice. Industry-standard synchronization requires expensive specialized hardware and complex setup, while data-driven alternatives including audio-based alignment, geometry matching, and pose tracking remain limited by restrictive environmental or scene-specific assumptions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Phase-DGS, a framework that replaces conventional timestamps with a semantic phase representing each frame's inherent state within the underlying motion cycle. Frames capturing the same motion state share the same phase regardless of which camera records them or when, naturally establishing spatiotemporal correspondence across unsynchronized cameras. We validate Phase-DGS under temporal offsets, frame drops, and camera freezes, achieving up to +8.5 dB PSNR improvement over baselines while enabling seamless integration with existing DGS backbones including RealTime-4DGS and FreeTimeGS.
